body.p: Applicant replies to the non-final Office Action dated May 9, 2022, in which this Reply is filed within three months. Claims 1-9, 11-12, and 14-2 1 stand rejected. Reconsideration is respectfully requested.
Applicant thanks the Examiner for the indication that claim 10 would be allowable if rewritten in independent form.
Rejections under Q 102
Claims 1-5, 7, 8, 11, and 12 are rejected under 102 as being anticipated by U.S. Patent No. 6,315,079 (Berends). Applicant traverses the rejection.

The standard for anticipation under 35 USC 102 is that every aspect of a claim must identically appear in a single prior art reference for it to anticipate the claim under 35 USC 102 (In re Bond, 15 USPQ2d 1566 (Fed. Cir. 1990)). "[T]here must be no difference between the claimed invention and the reference disclosure, as viewed by a person of ordinary skill in the field of the invention" (Scripps Clinic & Research Found, v. Genentech, Inc., 18 USPQ2d 1001, 1010 (Fed. Cir. 1991)).

"A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference." Verdegaal Bros v. Union Oil Co. of California, 814 F.2d 628, 631 (Fed. Cir. 1987). "The identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the ... claim." Richardson v. Suzuki Motor Co., 868 F.2d 1226, 1236 (Fed. Cir. 1989).

Unless a single prior art reference describes "all of the limitations claimed" and all of the limitations are arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim, it cannot be said to prove prior invention of the thing claimed and, thus, cannot anticipate under 35 U.S.C. @ 102. (See NetMoneyINlnc. v. VeriSign Inc., 545 F.3d 1359, 1371 (Fed. Cir. 2008)).

Berends generally discloses a vehicle lift system. For instance, the Berends system comprises "four separately displaceable lifting columns 2 which co-act to lift a bus 4." More specifically, the Berends system utilizes a hydraulic unit 11 for vertically (i.e., one dimension) displacing a carriage 7 with respect to a respective column 6 via a hydraulic cylinder 10. The Berends system utilizes a control means 14 for switching on and off hydraulic unit 11. The

Berends system further utilizes a push-bar 13 which can be moved up and downward in pumping manner to move wheels 12 downward relative to support foot 8 whereby lifting column 2 becomes displaceable on wheels 12. The Berends push-bar 13 is used for maneuvering the lifting column 2 in a mobile situation, and as addressed in the discussion of claim 17 below this movement of a given lifting column 2 is not while its support foot 8 is engaging/lifting the bus.

Significantly, Berends fails to disclose moving the lifting column 2 in two dimensions (e.g., horizontally, for instance along an x axis and then along a z axis, or vice versa) about a cargo deck in response to receiving instructions from a control module (e.g., control means 14). Instead, Berends is limited to only being moved in a single dimension (i.e., vertically) by displacing each lifting column 2 vertically with control means 14. (e.g., see col. 3, 11. 6-11 of Berends).
Therefore, Berends, alone or in combination with any of the cited references, fails to disclose or contemplate at least:

the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot configured to move in two different dimensions about the cargo deck in response to receiving instructions from a control module to move the cargo unit from the first position to the second position

as recited in independent claim 1 (emphasis added) and as similarly recited in independent claim 11. (Solely for clarification, claims 1 and 11 are amended to recite "two different dimensions). Claim 17 recites, "moving, via the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot, the cargo unit to the second position, wherein the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot transport the cargo unit horizontally about a cargo deck in response to moving from the first position to the second position." (Emphasis added). Applicant submits that the comments above with respect to claims 1 and 11 apply, mutatis mutandis, to independent claim 17. Applicant therefore respectfully submits that independent claims 1, 11, and 17 are allowable over the cited references.

Based upon the foregoing, claims 1, 11, and 17 are allowable over Berends. All claims that depend from claim 1, 11, or 17 are thereby also allowable over Berends for the above-noted reasons. There is therefore no need to separately address the patentability of each of these claims and/or the Patent Office's interpretation in relation to any of these claims or any of the references of record in relation thereto.
Rejections under @ 103
Claims 17-21 are rejected under 103 as being unpatentable over Berends. Applicant traverses the rejection.
The Examiner asserts:
Regarding claims 17-21, the recTted method steps for moving a cargounit Ts cons[dered to be

of the invention to have performed the claimed method by the apparatusof Berends et al. for the
purpose of providing an efficient means of moving a bus from one place to another.
(Office Action, page 4)
As discussed above with respect to the 102 rejection, Berends fails to disclose or contemplate at least:

moving, via the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot, the cargo unit to the second position, wherein the first cargo handling robot and the second cargo handling robot transport the cargo unit horizontally about a cargo deck in response to moving from the first position to the second position
as recited in independent claim 17 (emphasis added).

MPEP § 2143 states that "[t]he key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious. The Supreme Court in KSR noted that the analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit" (emphasis added). According to MPEP § 2143, rationales that may support a conclusion of obviousness include:
(A) Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results;
(B) Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results;
(C) Use of known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way;
(D) Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results;
(E) "Obvious to try" - choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success;

(F) Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art;

(G) Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.

While the above is not an all-inclusive list, the MPEP requires that some rationale be provided in order to support a conclusion of obviousness. In this case, not only has the Office Action failed to present one or more of the above-listed rationales, the Office Action has failed to present any type of reasonable rationale. In particular, the rejection lacks a clear articulation of the reasons why these features would allegedly have been obvious and, therefore, the rejection cannot be supported per the requirements set forth by the United States Supreme Court in the KSR decision. Although each column 12 of the lifting device 1 of Berends includes wheels 12 that may be used to transport a given column 12 from one location to another, nothing in Berends would disclose or suggest doing so while all four columns 12 are engaging the bus 4 (to move the bus 4 from one location on the ground to a different location on the ground), much less while the bus 4 is vertically spaced from the ground by the support foot 8 (of each of the four columns 12) engaging the bus 4 and by each such support foot 8 being vertically spaced from the ground. Thus, it is respectfully submitted that the rejection is improper and must be withdrawn. For example, how could the skilled person perform the claimed method by the apparatus of Berends if the system of Berends is limited to one dimensional vertical movement (i.e., vertical hydraulic lifting) using the control means 14. It is at least this type of consideration that the Examiner fails to address in the rejection that renders the rejection improper.
Applicant respectfully requests that the 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection of claim 17-21 over Berends be withdrawn in light of the above comments.

In view of the above remarks, Applicant respectfully submits that all pending claims are allowable and requests allowance of the pending claims.
